title: Alex Scott: From Guernsey to Bournemouth via an unorthodox road to the top
content:
After scoring the winning goal for Bournemouth against Premier League leaders Arsenal earlier this month, Alex Scott gave the impression he was sending a message to one person in particular.

Following celebrations with his team-mates in front of the away end at the Emirates Stadium, the 22-year-old central midfielder, who is one of the many players hoping to be named in England’s squad for the World Cup in June and July, mimed lifting an imaginary phone and then dramatically hanging up.

To some, it looked like Scott — who just six years ago was a teenager playing for non-League side Guernsey FC on the English Channel island — was mimicking dialling up England head coach Thomas Tuchel.

“I’ve been getting loads of messages about that,” Scott tells The Athletic, laughing, still giddy about it all. “But no, it had nothing to do with that. I love tennis, and Ben Shelton (the American who is sixth in that sport’s world rankings) does that celebration when he wins games sometimes, so that’s what it was.

“I can see maybe the confusion, but it had nothing to do with England.”

Scott is a welcome and familiar face in this area of Bournemouth’s £32million ($43m) training ground, opened a year ago, where interviews are conducted and various media duties carried out.

He will do anything for the club, staff say, and that certainly comes across during a 45-minute conversation with The Athletic about his international ambitions, the impending departure of head coach Andoni Iraola and his England Women family member, Maya Le Tissier. It was as if he had nowhere else to be.

Growing up, Scott was a Tottenham Hotspur fan, so, naturally, he revelled in scoring that goal against their bitter north London rivals. Ask Scott who he supports now, and he will tell you it is Bournemouth, the club he joined for £25million from Bristol City of the second-tier Championship in summer 2023.

As for calls, Scott is hoping to get a real one from Tuchel in the next month to say he has been selected for that World Cup squad.

The first time Tuchel contacted him was late last year, via FaceTime, to break the news that he had made the squad for the final round of World Cup qualifying fixtures in November.

“The call, first of all, was crazy. I just couldn’t wait to get off it to tell my family and friends,” Scott says. “It was on the Thursday night. The squad came out Friday, and then you get to go away with these players that you have grown up watching and idolising.”

Scott was not only in awe of the company he was keeping during that camp — Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane and Real Madrid midfielder Jude Bellingham to name but two — but also of the speed at which his first England training session was carried out.

He had Manchester City goalkeeper James Trafford and Nottingham Forest midfielder Elliot Anderson there for support, having played with them both internationally at youth level. Anderson, who has seven senior caps, and Scott had helped England retain the Under-21 European Championship last summer.

“It was like 100mph,” says Scott of that opening period of training under Tuchel. “I’ve never seen anything like that before. As the days go on, you get used to it and you feel more comfortable around the lads — but that first session, I’ll never forget that, it was ridiculous.

“The standard and the speed of the football was something I’ve never seen before, it’s frightening. But you’ve got to go in and just keep reminding yourself that you do belong at this level, (that) you’ve been picked for a reason.”

Scott did not make the matchday squad for a 2-0 defeat of Serbia at Wembley but was then an unused substitute for a win by the same scoreline away to Albania three days later. His family, including parents Steph and Noel, made the journey from Guernsey, an island around 30 miles off the north coast of France, to Tirana in the hope he would earn his first senior cap.

“It’s a shame I didn’t get on the pitch, but there’s plenty more camps ahead,” Scott says. “I’ve got to keep my head down and keep working hard for Bournemouth, and hopefully I get another call-up soon.”

Scott’s route from being the youngest player to play for Guernsey FC, in the eighth tier of English football at 16, to training with England is not the usual way to the top.

When he was 12, Scott was released by Southampton’s academy after four years. He spent a year training with Bournemouth, but with his confidence low and the back-and-forth flights from home to England’s south coast taking their toll, he left the club.

Scott says he was a typical teenager in those days. He wanted to be with his friends and play football with them. Leaving Bournemouth was his “most important decision” during a time when he put himself first.

But his talent was too prodigious to be lost. Soon enough, he was discovered playing, just having fun, he says, on the pitches of Guernsey’s capital, St Peter Port, his technical ability clear for all to see. At 16, he was invited to a trial at Bristol City.

“It was almost, like, now or never,” Scott reflects. “And to have that realisation, if you don’t go to this now, I think the professional footballer dream is definitely over. So I thought, ‘I might as well go, I still want to be a professional footballer. Go and see what happens. You never know what can happen’.”

And what happened?

“I scored a hat-trick on my trial, which was the perfect way to start. Then they offered me a contract after that, and I never really looked back,” Scott says, smiling again.

“After that, it all happened so quickly. Within a year and a bit, I was playing in the first team for Bristol City and in England Under-18s. Within the space of two years it was, ‘You’re here. Now you’re a professional footballer’.”

He is not the only one of those in the family, either. His step-sister, Maya Le Tissier, is a defender for Manchester United and England’s back-to-back European champion Lionesses. They grew up playing for the same Guernsey youth team, St. Martin’s AC.

“Everyone knew how good Maya was. She was our best player,” Scott says. “We knew she was going to go right to the very top. I don’t think many would have said the same about me.

“From the start, you could tell she was going to be a star; for me, it came a little bit later. She’s unbelievable and doing so well for United and for England. I speak to her pretty much every day. I couldn’t be prouder of her.”

Le Tissier was one of the people Scott leaned on for advice ahead of his first England camp.

Guernsey has a population of only around 66,000, so almost everybody on the island is familiar with the pair of them.

“People our age, they know us as normal people,” Scott says. “Obviously, the kids are different. When you go back and visit your old school and the kids are all there, it’s really nice to see and they see you as these superstars and idolise you. But, day to day, seeing people we’ve grown up with our whole lives, they just know us as Alex and Maya who grew up in Guernsey.”

The island is a self-governing British Crown Dependency, which means those born there are eligible to represent any of the home nations —England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland.

There is also another possibility for Scott. With dad Noel being from Dublin, he is also eligible to play for the Republic of Ireland. There has been some suggestion that they might try to persuade him to represent the nation of his father.

“I have not heard anything, or given it any thought,” Scott says. “I played for England throughout all the younger age groups, so, yeah, my focus at the minute is playing as well as I can for Bournemouth and trying to get in that England squad for the World Cup.”

Scott has played in all 34 of Bournemouth’s league games this season, starting all but three of them. After struggling with injuries in his first couple of seasons at the club, he feels he was able to win Iraola’s trust this term and has gone from strength to strength under the Spaniard’s tutelage.

But, just as their partnership finally got up and running, it was announced that Iraola is to step down at the end of this campaign after three years in charge.

“He pulled us in before training (to let us know), as I think everyone knew it was up in the air,” Scott says. “We didn’t know if he was staying or going, and he just let us know that it’ll be his final year here, which is obviously sad for us to hear.

“It’s football, though; managers come and go, players come and go. We’ll try our best for the new manager that comes in, but this manager has been brilliant for me, brought me in here (in his first transfer window in charge), gave me my Premier League debut and trusted me throughout this season. I’ll always be grateful to him for giving me my opportunity.

“The biggest influence he’s had on me is definitely tactically. He’s improved me as a player and taken me to a different level. When I came in, my tactical understanding was pretty much nothing, and that’s why maybe I didn’t play as much, as tactically I wasn’t good enough and physically I probably wasn’t at the level either.

“I’ve had to work on that, and Andoni and the coaching staff have helped me massively.”

Iraola’s style of play at Bournemouth revolves around a punishing pressing game, which is something that took Scott time to adjust to as the No 8 in midfield.

“At times, I didn’t know when to go (press). I was worried about what’s behind me,” Scott says. “He gives you that confidence just to go flat-out and the defenders behind you will know to come (and press) as well. That’s probably his main strength, I’d say, as a coach, and it’s a brilliant way of football, it’s really exciting.”

Scott, who Manchester City manager Pep Guardiola famously called an “unbelievable player”, has always been someone whose name has done the rounds on the transfer-rumour mill. Ever since he was tearing it up in the Championship for Bristol City with the nickname the ‘Guernsey (Jack) Grealish’, a tag he feels he has now respectfully outgrown, there has been a buzz that he will make it to the very top.

“Obviously, you hear it (the speculation); it’s impossible not to,” Scott says. “But, for me, the focus is on playing well until the end of the season and staying fit. My aim is to be playing in the World Cup in the summer. That’s the only thing on my mind.”

What Scott has already proven this season is that he is not waiting by the phone. He is already dialled in.
